title: Tyrannosaur Rex: A New Theory

paragraphs.text: Jack Horner is not your typical academic. He struggled hard at school. 'But I liked digging in the dirt when I was a little kid, and discovering things,' he remembers. 'My father owned a sand and gravel plant so he dug holes in the ground with big machinery. But he also knew quite a bit about geology and he remembered riding his horse across the prairie and seeing dinosaur bones actually sticking up out of the rock on his ranch in Montana. When I was eight, he took me back to the area and I picked up a piece of bone, which was the first piece of dinosaur bone I collected. I still have it,' he adds with a laugh, 'but I haven't a clue what it is.'

As a result of an impressive high school project on dinosaurs, Horner was invited to go to Montana University to do a degree in paleontology, the study of fossils, despite poor grades at high school. He was doubtful whether he'd cope, and indeed he gave up after a year. After two years he returned to persevere for another four years. 'At the end of that time, I decided I'd taken all the courses I wanted to take or needed. So I quit – without a degree.' Ironically, the university later awarded Horner an honorary Doctor of Science.

Horner applied to every museum he could think of and was offered jobs at three of them. He accepted a place at Princeton, because it was the smallest, and 'Los Angeles and Toronto sounded too big to me'. Since then he's become one of the world's foremost dinosaur experts. He found the first dinosaur eggs in the world, and the first embryos. He's the scientific consultant for all of the Hollywood Jurassic Park movies. It is widely accepted that the Dr. Alan character, played by Sam Neill, was largely modeled on Jack Horner. He laughs when I ask how this feels. 'I was very glad he didn't get eaten by the Tyrannosaurus Rex,' is all he'll say.

Horner's team has discovered most of the Tyrannosaurus Rex skeletons found in recent years, including the biggest, the oldest and the most complete. But as he learned more about the 'tyrant lizard king', Horner gradually became convinced that, far from hunting its own prey, T-Rex survived on the dead bodies that it found of animals killed catastrophically in large numbers, or by predators.

When I challenge him that T-Rex does share certain characteristics with predatory reptiles, like a big mouth full of sharp teeth, he disagrees: 'It's certainly got a big mouth full of teeth but they're blunt. They're suited to crushing bones. You need teeth as sharp as knives for killing prey.' When I mention its big hind legs, Horner explains that humans and other animals that are adapted for walking have longer bones at the top of the leg in the thigh and shorter bones at the bottom of the leg in the shin. This applies to T-Rex. On the other hand, creatures which run fast, such as the giant flightless bird the ostrich, or some of the big cats like the cheetah, have short thigh bones and long shin bones. Based on this, the leg bones of all predatory dinosaurs seem to be adapted for running, while T-Rex would seem to be a walker.

But the most convincing evidence, according to Horner, is the biomasses of T-Rex compared with other dinosaurs from the time. His ongoing project in Montana is an attempt to understand how the ecosystem worked there 65 million years ago. By calculating the biomass of T-Rex, it's possible to work out how many dinosaurs of each type co-existed. 'Animals that scavenge, that is, live on dead creatures that they find lying around, are much more common than predators, who hunt and kill their food, but still less common than the prey,' Horner explains. Horner's team found nine T-Rex specimens but no Dromaeosaurus Raptors, which are known to be the predators at the top of the pyramid. 'That's very strong evidence that T-Rex was not a predator,' says Horner. 'If you add up the biomass of T-Rex, it comes out at the same biomass as you get in the Serengeti National Park in Africa today with scavengers like hyenas and vultures.'

Horner is prepared to remain open-minded if someone comes up with convincing scientific evidence against his hypothesis. His main argument for those who think that T-Rex could have been part predator, part scavenger is that you still need some evidence for T-Rex being a predator, and he remains convinced that there is none. 'Science is about evidence, not egos,' he concludes. 'We have a preconceived idea that T-Rex was a hunter. No-one ever presented that as evidence to begin with. Just because it was mean looking doesn't make it a predator by default. This is the first hypothesis to be based on science. So, I'm not going against the grain, because there was no evidence to begin with. There was no original hypothesis.'

subtitle: Jack Horner is one of the world's foremost dinosaur experts, but his recent ideas about the dinosaur Tyrannosaurus Rex – otherwise known as T-Rex – have landed him in controversy. Sally Palmer interviews him
